about: Published rows where the reference package has fewer errors than Andrey, each with its cause. qa/reference_parity.py accepts an entry only when its cause is correct-by-paper, reference-defect, tie-break, or trade-off, it gives a reason and a citation, and it pins the row's current error values; a tie-break entry's evidence gives the row's error values with the columns in reversed order, or with the tie ranks reversed for a method whose result does not depend on the column order, where the row passes.

entries.reason: causal-learn's FCI output depends on the process hash seed. Its possible-d-sep step walks a Python set of graph nodes hashed by name, which Python randomizes per process, and it decides membership while the walk is still growing, so the order changes which edges it removes. On the series that differs, causal-learn returns Andrey's graph under four of six hash seeds; the published value is one draw. Andrey's possible-d-sep sets in this build follow the column order, which is also a tie-break rather than a rule error.
entries.citation: causal-learn 0.1.4.8 (MIT): causallearn/graph/GraphNode.py, GraphNode.__hash__ returns hash(self.name); causallearn/search/ConstraintBased/FCI.py, getPossibleDsep iterates set(graph.get_adjacent_nodes(x)). Possible-D-Sep: Spirtes, P., Glymour, C., and Scheines, R. (2000). Causation, Prediction, and Search, 2nd ed. MIT Press.

entries.reason: Two series differ. On seed 0, Andrey applies rule R4 on every sweep until no rule applies, as Zhang (2008) states; causal-learn runs R4 only in a sweep where R1-R3 changed a mark, so it skips one R4 step that Andrey takes; there a finite-sample independence test makes one endpoint wrong. Skipping R4 this way changes the output on 1 of 721 latent_gauss_er datasets. On seed 1, the difference is the possible-d-sep visit order: causal-learn's result depends on the process hash seed (see the d = 50 entry), and Andrey's falls inside the range of causal-learn's draws.
entries.citation: Zhang, J. (2008). On the completeness of orientation rules for causal discovery in the presence of latent confounders and selection bias. Artificial Intelligence 172(16-17), 1873-1896. causal-learn 0.1.4.8 (MIT): causallearn/search/ConstraintBased/FCI.py, the orientation loop and getPossibleDsep.

entries.reason: The two packages optimize different scores. Andrey's hill climbing maximizes the BIC with the maximum-likelihood residual variance, as Schwarz (1978) and Chickering (2002) define it. bnlearn's Gaussian BIC divides each node's residual sum of squares by n - p - 1, where p is the node's parent count, which adds a small cost per parent. On both series that differ, the searches end one edge apart: the last edge Andrey adds improves the maximum-likelihood BIC, and bnlearn's estimator rejects it, so Andrey's graph has the lower BIC by the paper's definition. With bnlearn's estimator patched into Andrey's search, it returns bnlearn's equivalence class on all 35 series of the lane.
entries.citation: Schwarz, G. (1978). Estimating the dimension of a model. Annals of Statistics 6(2), 461-464. Chickering, D. M. (2002). Optimal structure identification with greedy search. JMLR 3, 507-554.

entries.reason: lingam's pruning step builds the lag-1 columns of its regression with np.roll, so its first regression row pairs x(1) with x(T) and e(T), values from the end of the series that are not its past. The model defines the regression only where the lagged values are observed, so Andrey starts the regressions at the first step with a full lag. On this row all 10 series differ, and each differs only through that row: with lingam's residuals and causal order, Andrey's pruning with lingam's wrapped row returns lingam's graph on all 10, and without it Andrey's graph. The row has no consistent effect on accuracy: across the 54 series of the lane where it changes the graph, on identical residuals and order, dropping it has fewer errors on 18, keeping it on 18, and 18 tie.

(2010). Estimation of a structural vector autoregression model using non-Gaussianity. JMLR 11, 1709-1731, Sect. 2.1-2.2, Eqs. (1) and (3): x(t) regressed on x(t - tau) for observed t = 1, ..., T. Kawahara, Y., Shimizu, S., and Washio, T. (2011). Analyzing relationships among ARMA processes based on non-Gaussianity of external influences. Neurocomputing 74(12-13), 2212-2221.

entries.reason: The one series where tigramite has fewer errors differs only in the order of candidate separating sets. tigramite orders candidates using a memory updated while a group of links is tested, so its order follows the variable indices; Andrey orders by the memory as it stood when the group started, which does not depend on column order. Over 20 random column orders of that series, Andrey returns the same graph every time; tigramite matches Andrey's error count in 18 orders and has one fewer error in 2, so its advantage on this row comes from the column order of the stored data.
entries.citation: Gerhardus and Runge (2020), High-recall causal discovery for autocorrelated time series with latent confounders, NeurIPS; Supplement S5 (Algorithm S2 line 7; order-independent separating sets).

entries.method: GES on mixed data, degenerate Gaussian score
entries.reason: Andrey runs GES as Chickering defines it: each forward step takes the Insert with the largest score gain, then the backward phase deletes, and the result is a local optimum of those operators, which a check over every single-edge addition and removal in the equivalence class confirms. Two series differ. On one, Tetrad's FGES, which first scores only pairs whose marginal edge improves the score and then repeats its forward and backward passes, reaches a different local optimum that scores better under Andrey's degenerate Gaussian score; Tetrad's later release, whose score orders parent sets as Andrey's does, also reaches a better one. On the other, Andrey's graph has the better score under both packages' scores, so Tetrad's fewer errors there come from a lower-scoring graph, and Tetrad's later release returns Andrey's graph. The benchmarked Tetrad release's degenerate Gaussian score also differs from the paper's: it scores each indicator column of a categorical child on the parents alone, without the chain rule over the child's indicators.
entries.citation: Chickering, D. M. (2002). Optimal structure identification with greedy search. JMLR 3, 507-554. Ramsey, J., Glymour, M., Sanchez-Romero, R., and Glymour, C. (2017). A million variables and more: the fast greedy equivalence search algorithm. IJDSA 3(2), 121-129. Andrews, B., Ramsey, J., and Cooper, G. F. (2019). Learning high-dimensional directed acyclic graphs with mixed data-types. PMLR 104, 4-21. Tetrad 7.6.3 (GPL), tetrad-lib edu/cmu/tetrad/search/score/DegenerateGaussianScore.java, localScore; Tetrad 7.6.10, the same file, and edu/cmu/tetrad/search/Fges.java, search.

entries.method: Hill climbing on discrete data, BDeu score
entries.reason: Both packages run hill climbing on the same BDeu score: every pgmpy move changes the score by Andrey's change times -1/2, so they rank the moves alike. On every series of the row, the two searches first differ at a tie between adding x -> y and adding y -> x, which score equivalence makes exact: Andrey takes the addition with the lower column pair, pgmpy the first maximal move in its own move order. From there each search ends at a different local optimum of the same score, where no single addition, removal, or reversal improves it, and bnlearn's hill climbing returns Andrey's graph on every series. Hill climbing takes the best move and leaves ties open, so neither optimum is wrong by the method; on the four series where pgmpy has fewer errors, pgmpy's optimum scores better on all four. With the columns in reversed order, which reverses Andrey's tie-break, pgmpy has fewer errors on one series and Andrey on one, and Andrey returns pgmpy's graph on three of the five.
entries.citation: Chickering, D. M., Geiger, D., and Heckerman, D. (1995). Learning Bayesian networks: search methods and experimental results. AISTATS, 112-128. Heckerman, D., Geiger, D., and Chickering, D. M. (1995). Learning Bayesian networks: the combination of knowledge and statistical data. Machine Learning 20(3), 197-243 (score equivalence). pgmpy 1.1.2 (MIT): pgmpy/estimators/HillClimbSearch.py, _legal_operations enumerates the candidate additions from a set of ordered variable pairs, and estimate takes max(..., key=lambda t: t[1]), the first maximal move in that order.

entries.reason: On every dataset where the two outputs differ, the difference starts at one node's first grow step. There the p-values of several candidates underflow to exactly 0 in bnlearn, which takes the first column among them. Andrey takes the candidate with the strongest test statistic, the association measure that IAMB maximizes. Applied in Andrey's search, bnlearn's choice reproduces bnlearn's skeleton on all 4 differing datasets. Two of them have skeletons that differ and carry +7 of the row's +10 pairs; the other two have equal skeletons and carry +3, from Meek's rules on a cyclic partially directed graph and from a collider that bnlearn skips for closing a directed cycle.
entries.citation: Tsamardinos, I., Aliferis, C. F., and Statnikov, A. (2003). Algorithms for large scale Markov blanket discovery. FLAIRS, 376-380: the forward phase admits the variable that maximizes a heuristic function f(X ; T | CMB), a measure of association, not a p-value. bnlearn 5.2.1, traced through ia.markov.blanket: candidates whose p-value is 0 are taken in column order.

entries.reason: At 200 variables MMPC's forward step often faces candidates whose dependence is too strong to rank by p-value: the p-values underflow to exactly 0 in bnlearn, which takes the first column among them. Andrey takes the candidate with the strongest test statistic, the tie rule of the paper. That candidate is a true neighbor in 2,376 of 2,384 first picks (99.7%) against 1,176 (49%) for the first column, and the p-value key (no underflow) gives the same forward sets in 4,000 of 4,000 nodes. The extra errors are false edges between unrelated pairs (95% join variables in different components of the true graph or 5 or more steps apart) whose statistic is just past the cutoff (z 2.0 to 3.1; the cutoff is 1.96). An arbitrary pick admits a strongly correlated non-neighbor that removes some of them by chance, and the strongest-first rule keeps 44 such edges the other order removes, about 2 per graph. bnlearn's column-order pick, applied in Andrey's search, gives 843 errors on the 10 datasets of the rerun against bnlearn's recorded 842.
entries.citation: Tsamardinos, I., Brown, L. E., and Aliferis, C. F. (2006). The max-min hill-climbing Bayesian network structure learning algorithm. Machine Learning 65(1), 31-78: the forward phase admits the candidate whose weakest association with the target is the strongest, and the association measure orders candidates whose p-values saturate. bnlearn 5.2.1: candidates whose p-value is 0 are taken in column order.

entries.reason: The two packages run different discrete tests. Andrey's chi-square test takes the exact permutation mean of the statistic as its degrees of freedom, so a sparse table keeps its level. bnlearn's x2-adf adjusts the degrees of freedom by a rule for sparse tables. On 3,840 random triples from child, insurance, alarm, and hepar2 the two decisions at alpha 0.05 agree in 97.7%, falling to 92% with 3 conditioning variables, and the graphs are not equal on any of the 3,183 datasets of those four networks (595 of 790 on asia). hepar2 has the largest conditioning sets, where the disagreement is widest.
entries.citation: Tsamardinos, I., and Borboudakis, G. (2010). Permutation testing improves Bayesian network learning. ECML PKDD, 322-337: the statistic's degrees of freedom are its exact permutation mean. bnlearn 5.2.1: ci.test with test x2-adf.

entries.reason: With three or more environments, the approximate test compares each environment's residuals with the other rows' and takes the smallest of the K p-values times K, the paper's Bonferroni correction; InvariantCausalPrediction multiplies by K - 1, below the Bonferroni factor at K >= 3 (with two environments both use 1, as the two comparisons are one). Andrey therefore accepts a superset of the reference's sets and names fewer variables: on all 21 of this row's 500 paired fits that differ, Andrey's parents are a subset of the reference's. At 6 nodes that costs 0.024 errors per fit, all from parents not named (missed 1.592 against 1.556 per fit), while the share of fits naming a non-parent is 0.010 against 0.018; at 10 nodes the same correction gives Andrey fewer errors, 0.406 against 0.420 per fit.
entries.citation: Peters, J., Buhlmann, P., and Meinshausen, N. (2016). Causal inference by using invariant prediction: identification and confidence intervals. JRSS-B 78(5), 947-1012, Section 3.1 (Method II, Bonferroni over the K environments). InvariantCausalPrediction 0.8 (GPL): R/getpval.R, pval <- min(pvalvec) * (length(IN) - 1).

entries.reason: Andrey centers every column before the fit, the same as fitting an intercept. The paper's loss has no intercept, so it cannot fit the mean of the noise the paper's simulations draw, exponential of scale 1 and mean 1; centering is the default for that reason. On that noise Andrey makes fewer errors than CausalNex in 5 of the 10 settings, each replicated on seeds 20-39, and no more in the other 5. On noise of mean 0, as in this row, the means the centering estimates are 0, and estimating them costs one degree of freedom per variable, about one time step of data. That cost shows only where the fit has more weights than steps: at 100 variables and 50 steps, Andrey makes 3.20 more errors than CausalNex on seeds 0-19 [+0.10, +6.00] and 4.15 more on seeds 20-39 [+1.30, +7.10], of about 150. On those 40 series Andrey's fit without centering makes 3.50 fewer errors (95% interval 1.48 to 5.50) and ties CausalNex once rerun (+0.65 [+0.05, +1.35] on seeds 0-19, -0.30 [-1.00, +0.35] on seeds 20-39); a fit not centered on 49 of the 50 steps makes 3.25 more errors [+0.50, +6.30] than on all 50.
entries.citation: Pamfil, R., et al. (2020). DYNOTEARS: Structure learning from time-series data. AISTATS, PMLR 108, Appendix B.4: noise drawn from exponential distributions of scale 1, as in NOTEARS (Zheng et al. 2018). benchmarks/published/0.14.0/dynotears.json: centering.

entries.reason: At alpha 1e-4 and n = 1000 the IGSP objective (arrows, then I-contradicting arrows) often ties or ranks a wrong DAG at or below the true one: over the 100 draws per seed block (20 datasets, 5 draws), the true DAG's objective equals the returned DAG's in 42 and 26 and is strictly higher in 45 and 65. Both packages compute the same objective on every DAG compared (Andrey's and the reference's DAG in 200 of 200 draws). Andrey's first start is the minimum-degree order with its ties broken by Andrey's tie ranks, the same in every draw, and a later start replaces its result only with a strictly lower objective; the reference draws all five starts at random in every draw. On the datasets where the first start lands on the worse member of an exact objective tie, or in a worse basin that the other four starts miss, all five Andrey draws repeat that outcome. Per start, the two searches reach the best basin equally often (31% and 32% on the largest contributor), and their random start orders give the same outcomes. With the tie ranks reversed the row passes on both seed blocks (seeds 100-119: 2.59 against 2.76; seeds 0-19: 2.28 against 2.12, interval [-0.03, 0.37]), and with 20 random rankings it is worse on both blocks for none. At Andrey's default of 10 starts the row ties (+0.13, interval [-0.07, 0.34]).

ICML, PMLR 80, 5537-5546 (Algorithm 1: restarts from minimum-degree orders, ties left open). Solus, L., Wang, Y., and Uhler, C. (2021). Consistency guarantees for greedy permutation-based causal inference algorithms. Biometrika 108(4), 795-814. graphical-model-learning 0.1a8: graphical_model_learning/algorithms/dag/gsp.py, igsp (min_degree_alg_amat with random.choice ties in every run).

evidence.note: Seeds 100-119, the row's replication. Andrey's igsp does not depend on the column order, so its tie ranks are reversed.

entries.reason: Both packages compute the same G-square statistic and count its degrees of freedom differently on sparse tables: Andrey refers it to the statistic's mean when one variable is shuffled within each configuration, bnlearn's mi-adf to (r_x - 1)(r_y - 1) summed over the configurations, counting the values present. With mi-adf's degrees of freedom in Andrey's search, which degrees_of_freedom="nonempty" gives (the same sets on all 740 targets of seeds 0-19), Andrey returns bnlearn's sets on 97% of the targets and ties it on both seed halves (distance -0.0009 [-0.0043, +0.0025] and +0.0007 [-0.0021, +0.0040]); bnlearn's sparse-table rule and each rule where its search differs from the paper's Fig. 1 move the difference by at most 0.002. The paper orders candidates by the significance of a G-square test and gives no degrees of freedom. The same swap turns Andrey's lead at 1,000 rows into a tie on child (distance -0.068 -> -0.001), cuts it on hepar2 (-0.034 -> -0.004), and turns it into a deficit on insurance (-0.018 -> +0.005): on child, mi-adf's degrees of freedom reject up to 13.5% of the true independences at level 0.05.
entries.citation: Yaramakala, S. and Margaritis, D. (2005). Speculative Markov blanket discovery for optimal feature selection. ICDM, Fig. 1, and p. 3: h is the significance of a G-square test; no degrees of freedom are given. bnlearn 5.2.1 (GPL): the mi-adf test (adjusted degrees of freedom).

entries.reason: The difference is the candidates of each round. The paper's line 24 tests every variable outside the blanket given it, and Andrey's search does; bnlearn's fast.iamb drops from its pool every variable that was in the blanket at the end of a round, so a variable a later shrink removes is never tested again. A trace running one Fisher z test (bnlearn's zf agrees to 5e-7) under ports of both searches, with every rule switchable, reproduces Andrey's records on every target and bnlearn's on 1,976 to 1,998 of 2,000 per seed half. With bnlearn's pool rule in Andrey's search the difference is 0.0000 to -0.0002 on both seed halves at 1,000 and 5,000 rows, and with Andrey's rule in bnlearn's search the gap returns; the batch order, the shrink, and the stop move nothing. At all but one of the 333 targets where the two differ, the first difference is a variable that left the blanket in a shrink and tests dependent again given the current blanket; where it stays in Andrey's set it is outside the true blanket in 171 of 174 cases at 1,000 rows and 140 of 141 at 5,000. On the graphs with 50 variables and mean degree 4 at 1,000 rows the paper's rule gives the smaller distance, by 0.003.
entries.citation: Yaramakala, S. and Margaritis, D. (2005). Speculative Markov blanket discovery for optimal feature selection. ICDM, Fig. 1, line 24: S <- {A | A in U - {T} - B(T) and A dependent on T given B(T)}. bnlearn 5.2.1 (GPL): R/fast-iamb.R, fast.ia.markov.blanket, nodes = nodes[nodes %!in% mb] at the end of each round.

entries.reason: The difference is the candidates of each round. The paper's line 24 tests every variable outside the blanket given it, and Andrey's search does; bnlearn's fast.iamb drops from its pool every variable that was in the blanket at the end of a round, so a variable a later shrink removes is never tested again. A trace running one Fisher z test (bnlearn's zf agrees to 5e-7) under ports of both searches, with every rule switchable, reproduces Andrey's records on every target and bnlearn's on 1,976 to 1,998 of 2,000 per seed half. With bnlearn's pool rule in Andrey's search the difference is 0.0000 to -0.0002 on both seed halves at 1,000 and 5,000 rows, and with Andrey's rule in bnlearn's search the gap returns; the batch order, the shrink, and the stop move nothing. At all but one of the 333 targets where the two differ, the first difference is a variable that left the blanket in a shrink and tests dependent again given the current blanket; where it stays in Andrey's set it is outside the true blanket in 171 of 174 cases at 1,000 rows and 140 of 141 at 5,000. On the graphs with 50 variables and mean degree 4 at 1,000 rows the paper's rule gives the smaller distance, by 0.003.
